questions.question: Distinguish scalar and vector quantities and give two examples of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Scalars have magnitude only, e.g. speed, distance, mass, time. Vectors have magnitude and direction, e.g. velocity, displacement, force, acceleration.
markingPoints: Scalars have magnitude only, e.g. speed, distance, mass, time. Vectors have magnitude and direction, e.g. velocity, displacement, force, acceleration.

questions.question: Classify friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force, gravity, electrostatic force and magnetic force as contact or non-contact.
questions.modelAnswer: Contact: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact. Non-contact: gravity, electrostatic and magnetic forces.
markingPoints: Contact: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact. Non-contact: gravity, electrostatic and magnetic forces.

questions.question: Explain what a resultant force is.
questions.modelAnswer: A single force with the same effect as all forces acting together; it is the vector sum of the forces.
markingPoints: A single force with the same effect as all forces acting together
it is the vector sum of the forces.

questions.question: State three rules for drawing a free-body diagram.
questions.modelAnswer: Represent the object as a box or point; draw labelled force arrows from the object; arrow direction shows direction and arrow length should represent magnitude.
markingPoints: Represent the object as a box or point
draw labelled force arrows from the object
arrow direction shows direction and arrow length should represent magnitude.

questions.question: Distinguish mass from weight.
questions.modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kg and is a scalar. Weight is the gravitational force on a mass, measured in N, is a vector and depends on gravitational field strength.
markingPoints: Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kg and is a scalar. Weight is the gravitational force on a mass, measured in N, is a vector and depends on gravitational field strength.

questions.question: Explain the link between work done and energy transfer.
questions.modelAnswer: When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done; the work done equals the energy transferred.
markingPoints: When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done
the work done equals the energy transferred.

questions.question: Distinguish elastic deformation from inelastic deformation.
questions.modelAnswer: Elastic deformation reverses when the force is removed; inelastic deformation is permanent; the object does not return fully to its original shape.
markingPoints: Elastic deformation reverses when the force is removed
the object does not return fully to its original shape.

questions.question: State Hooke’s law and the condition under which it applies.
questions.modelAnswer: Extension is directly proportional to force; this applies only up to the limit of proportionality.
markingPoints: Extension is directly proportional to force
this applies only up to the limit of proportionality.

questions.question: State the principle of moments for an object in equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: Total clockwise moment about a pivot equals total anticlockwise moment about that pivot.
markingPoints: Total clockwise moment about a pivot equals total anticlockwise moment about that pivot.

questions.question: Explain how a lever can act as a force multiplier.
questions.modelAnswer: A small force is applied farther from the pivot; its moment equals a larger force acting closer to the pivot; increasing perpendicular distance increases moment.
markingPoints: A small force is applied farther from the pivot
its moment equals a larger force acting closer to the pivot

questions.question: Explain why liquid pressure increases with depth.
questions.modelAnswer: There is a taller column of liquid above; its weight is greater; therefore force per unit area and pressure are greater.
markingPoints: There is a taller column of liquid above
therefore force per unit area and pressure are greater.

questions.question: Explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude.
questions.modelAnswer: There is less air above; the air column has less weight and density is lower; fewer particle collisions produce less pressure.
markingPoints: the air column has less weight and density is lower
fewer particle collisions produce less pressure.

questions.question: State Newton’s first law.
questions.modelAnswer: If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object remains stationary and a moving object continues at constant velocity.
markingPoints: If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object remains stationary and a moving object continues at constant velocity.

questions.question: State Newton’s second law.
questions.modelAnswer: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass; F = ma.
markingPoints: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass

questions.question: State Newton’s third law and clarify where the two forces act.
questions.modelAnswer: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other; the forces act on different objects.
markingPoints: When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other
the forces act on different objects.

questions.question: State the two parts of stopping distance.
questions.modelAnswer: Thinking distance plus braking distance.

questions.question: Explain how tiredness and wet roads affect stopping distance.
questions.modelAnswer: Tiredness increases reaction time, so thinking distance increases. Wet roads reduce tyre-road friction, reducing braking force and increasing braking distance.
markingPoints: Tiredness increases reaction time, so thinking distance increases. Wet roads reduce tyre-road friction, reducing braking force and increasing braking distance.

questions.question: Explain how a falling object reaches terminal velocity.
questions.modelAnswer: Initially weight exceeds drag, so it accelerates. As speed rises, drag rises. Eventually drag equals weight, resultant force becomes zero, acceleration becomes zero and speed stays constant.
markingPoints: Initially weight exceeds drag, so it accelerates. As speed rises, drag rises. Eventually drag equals weight, resultant force becomes zero, acceleration becomes zero and speed stays constant.

questions.question: Define momentum and state its unit.
questions.modelAnswer: Momentum = mass × velocity; kg m/s.

questions.question: State the law of conservation of momentum.
questions.modelAnswer: In a closed system, total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after it.
markingPoints: In a closed system, total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after it.

questions.question: Explain how an airbag reduces the force on a passenger in a collision.
questions.modelAnswer: The passenger’s momentum changes to zero; the airbag increases the time over which the change occurs; force = change in momentum ÷ time; so the mean force is reduced.
markingPoints: The passenger’s momentum changes to zero
the airbag increases the time over which the change occurs
so the mean force is reduced.

questions.question: Calculate the weight of a 65 kg person where g = 9.8 N/kg.
A force of 120 N moves a box 3.5 m in the force direction. Calculate the work done.
A force of 18 N extends a spring by 0.060 m. Calculate the spring constant.
A perpendicular force of 35 N acts 0.40 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.
A force of 900 N acts over an area of 0.030 m². Calculate the pressure.
Calculate the pressure due to 2.5 m of water. Use density = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg.
A car changes velocity from 5.0 m/s to 23 m/s in 6.0 s. Calculate its acceleration.
A 1,500 kg car accelerates at 2.4 m/s². Calculate the resultant force.
Calculate the momentum of a 0.15 kg ball moving at 24 m/s.
A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s sticks to a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. Calculate their shared velocity.
questions.modelAnswer:
Total momentum before = (2.0 × 3.0) + (1.0 × 0) = 6.0 kg m/s
Total mass after = 3.0 kg
v = p ÷ m
v = 6.0 ÷ 3.0
v = 2.0 m/s

questions.question: Describe how to investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
questions.modelAnswer: Measure original spring length. Add known masses one at a time and calculate force using W = mg. Measure new length and calculate extension. Repeat readings, stay below elastic limit and plot force against extension. Control the same spring and measure at eye level beside a fixed ruler.
markingPoints: Measure original spring length. Add known masses one at a time and calculate force using W = mg. Measure new length and calculate extension. Repeat readings, stay below elastic limit and plot force against extension. Control the same spring and measure at eye level beside a fixed ruler.

questions.question: Describe an investigation of how force affects acceleration for a trolley of constant mass.
questions.modelAnswer: Use a trolley on a level runway attached over a pulley to a hanging mass. Use light gates/motion sensor to measure acceleration. Keep total system mass constant by moving masses from trolley to hanger, increasing pulling force. Repeat and plot acceleration against force. Reduce friction or measure/allow for it.
markingPoints: Use a trolley on a level runway attached over a pulley to a hanging mass. Use light gates/motion sensor to measure acceleration. Keep total system mass constant by moving masses from trolley to hanger, increasing pulling force. Repeat and plot acceleration against force. Reduce friction or measure/allow for it.

questions.question: A car travels at 12 m/s for 8 s, then at 20 m/s for 5 s. Calculate total distance.
questions.modelAnswer:
distance = area under a velocity–time graph
d₁ = 12 × 8 = 96 m
d₂ = 20 × 5 = 100 m
total = 196 m
markingPoints: distance = area under a velocity–time graph

questions.question: A 0.25 kg ball changes velocity from +18 m/s to −12 m/s in 0.060 s. Calculate the mean force.
questions.modelAnswer:
Δp = m(v − u)
Δp = 0.25 × (−12 − 18) = −7.5 kg m/s
F = Δp ÷ t
F = −7.5 ÷ 0.060 = −125 N
Magnitude 125 N, opposite to initial motion
markingPoints: Magnitude 125 N, opposite to initial motion
